passage: On stream selection day, the Class 10 corridor smelled of fresh photocopies. The form had three boxes: Science, Commerce, Humanities. Preeti's pen hovered over Humanities; she'd topped history every year and filled two notebooks with essays nobody had asked for. Then she looked around. Vijay, Anu, the whole lunch group were ticking Science. "Everyone good goes science," Vijay said, not even looking up. Preeti's stomach knotted. If she ticked Humanities, she'd be in a different building next year, eating lunch with strangers, the girl who couldn't handle science. Her palms were damp. She ticked Science, folded the form quickly, and handed it to the class teacher before she could change her mind. On the way out she passed the humanities noticeboard and didn't look at it.

qa.q: Which subject had Preeti topped every year?
qa.a: She'd topped history every year.

qa.q: What do Preeti's knotted stomach and damp palms suggest?
qa.a: They suggest she felt anxious about standing out, picturing lunch with strangers and being called the girl who couldn't handle science. 😰

qa.q: What could Preeti do before the forms are finalised?
qa.a: She could talk to a teacher or parent about what she really loves and ask whether she can still change her stream.

qa.q: How might Vijay's quick 'Everyone good goes science' land for others choosing?
qa.a: Said so casually, it makes any other choice sound second-best, which can push classmates like Preeti to follow the crowd.

grounding: A teenager picks science because her whole group does, though she loves history, anxious about standing out.

passage:
Dear Leela,
You asked why I sounded so tired on the phone. It's the streak thing. In my class, everyone posts a photo of their study desk at 3 am, every night, with a counter: Day 12, Day 20. Whoever breaks the streak gets teased in the group chat. I didn't want to start. I don't even study well that late; I just stare at the page. But when the whole class was doing it and I wasn't, it felt like a spotlight on my empty square. So I started. I'm on Day 9. My eyes burn in first period, and yesterday I fell asleep on the bus and missed my stop.
I know it's silly. I just can't be the only one who stops.
Chetan

qa.q: What day of the streak is Chetan on?
qa.a: Chetan is on Day 9.

qa.q: Why did Chetan start the streak despite not studying well that late?
qa.a: With the whole class posting, Chetan felt a spotlight on the empty square and was anxious about being the only one left out.

qa.q: What could help Chetan stop without feeling alone?
qa.a: Chetan could find one or two classmates who also hate it and quit together, and tell a parent or teacher how tired it's making them.

qa.q: How might Leela feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Leela may feel worried about Chetan falling asleep on the bus, and glad to have been told the real reason for the tiredness.

grounding: A teenager joins a late-night study streak because the whole class does it and fears being the only one who stops.

passage: Nazia, you'll laugh, but I have to tell you about the shoes. In September, three girls in my section came to school in those chunky white sneakers with the thick soles. By October it was fifteen. By November, I was the only one in Class 9 B in plain black school shoes. Nobody said anything, honestly. But I felt like everyone was looking at my feet. I'm Shreya, the one who used to say trends are silly. I begged Mummy for a week. She finally bought them, and they pinch, and I actually think they look like boats. I wore them anyway, every day. And then in January, half the class switched to canvas shoes. Guess what I asked for.

qa.q: How many in Shreya's section had the chunky sneakers by October?
qa.a: By October it was fifteen.

qa.q: Why did Shreya beg for shoes that pinch and look like boats?
qa.a: Being the only one in plain black shoes made Shreya feel watched and anxious, so fitting in mattered more than comfort or taste.

qa.q: What question could Shreya ask before asking for the canvas shoes?
qa.a: Shreya could ask, 'Would I still want these if nobody in class had them?' before deciding.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the canvas shoe request after the sneakers?
qa.a: Mummy may feel frustrated or amused, having given in after a week of begging for shoes Shreya now wants to replace.

grounding: A teenager begs for the sneakers the whole section wears, despite disliking them, then chases the next trend.

passage:
I'm Nandini, Sunaina's cousin, and we go to the same dance academy in Jaipur. Sunaina has done Kathak since she was six. She's good. Her teacher says she has "clean feet."
This term, almost every girl her age moved to the new hip-hop batch. Their videos were all over the class group. By the third week Sunaina was the only fifteen-year-old left in Kathak, standing between the little kids.
She started biting her nails before class. On Friday she asked me, very quietly, "Do I look weird in there?" On Monday her name was on the hip-hop list.
I watched her first hip-hop class through the glass. She kept checking the others and copying a beat late. When they all laughed, she laughed too, a second after.
I can't say what she really wanted. But she hasn't mentioned Kathak since, and her ghungroos are still in her bag.

qa.q: How old was Sunaina when she started Kathak?
qa.a: She has done Kathak since she was six.

qa.q: What was Sunaina worried about when she asked, 'Do I look weird in there?'
qa.a: She seemed anxious about standing out as the only fifteen-year-old left in Kathak among the little kids, while everyone her age had moved to hip-hop.

qa.q: What small step could Sunaina try to make a choice that is really hers?
qa.a: She could try one hip-hop class alongside Kathak for a few weeks and then ask herself which she would pick if nobody from the class group were watching.

qa.q: How does Nandini see the change in Sunaina?
qa.a: Nandini seems a little sad and unsure, noticing Sunaina copying a beat late and laughing a second after, and the ghungroos still in the bag.

grounding: Told by a cousin, it shows a teenager switching to what most peers chose, driven by anxiety about standing out.

passage:
Monday. Everyone in Yusuf's class had started playing the same online battle game at night. At lunch they talked only about last night's rounds. Yusuf, fifteen, didn't even like shooting games; he preferred his football and his sketchbook. He sat at the edge of the conversation, laughing when they laughed.
Wednesday. He downloaded the game. By eleven he was still playing, his eyes stinging. When his older sister Reena knocked, he said, "Everyone plays till one. If I don't, I'm the only one who has no idea what they're talking about."
"Do you like it?"
He shrugged, eyes still on the screen.
The next Monday. At lunch he could finally join in, and he told his story loudly. But in maths he nodded off twice, and his sketchbook stayed in his bag all week. That night Reena noticed him staring at the game's loading screen for a long time before he pressed play.

qa.q: How late did Yusuf say everyone plays?
qa.a: Everyone plays till one.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf keep playing a game he didn't even like?
qa.a: He felt anxious about being the only one with no idea what the others were talking about, so fitting in mattered more than enjoying it.

qa.q: What could Yusuf try to stay connected without giving up his sleep and sketching?
qa.a: He could play a few rounds early in the evening, or on weekends, and share his sketches or football with the friends who like them, so he isn't choosing only what the group does.

qa.q: How does Reena seem to see her brother's change over the week?
qa.a: Reena seems concerned, noticing her brother is tired, has stopped sketching, and hesitates at the loading screen as if part of him doesn't want to play.

grounding: Across three beats it shows a teenager following a game trend because many peers do, anxious about standing out, at a cost to sleep and hobbies.

passage:
School counsellor's note, stream selection week, Class 10
Zainab came in today with the form half filled: science, like her whole friend group. When I asked what subjects she enjoys, she named history and economics without hesitating, then quickly added, "But everyone's taking science. If I don't, I'll be the only one in a different class." She said the group chat is full of science-coaching plans and she feels sick imagining eating lunch alone. Her friend Samir, she said, told her humanities was "for people who can't do maths." She scored higher in maths than he did. We talked about the difference between choosing a subject and choosing a lunch table. She asked for a day to think and to talk to her parents. I will meet her again on Thursday.

qa.q: Which subjects does Zainab enjoy?
qa.a: History and economics.

qa.q: Why is Zainab about to choose science?
qa.a: She feels anxious about standing out and eating lunch alone, so following the friend group feels safer than choosing what she enjoys.

qa.q: What did the counsellor help Zainab separate, and why does it help?
qa.a: Choosing a subject from choosing a lunch table, so the decision is about her interests and not only the group.

qa.q: How might Samir's comment have affected Zainab?
qa.a: It probably made her feel more pressured and a bit small, even though she scored higher in maths than he did.

grounding: A counsellor records a teenage girl about to choose a stream because her whole group has, anxious about being the only one in a different class.

passage:
Saturday night
The whole class is doing the umbrella dance trend. Every single person has posted one. Even Sachin, who hates dancing, posted his yesterday with his little brother. My feed is just umbrellas.
I don't want to do it. I feel stupid dancing and I hate how I look in videos. But today at lunch Meghna said, "Usha's the only one left," and everyone laughed, and I laughed too, and my stomach felt like it was folding.
So tonight I filmed it eleven times in the bathroom. I posted the least bad one. Twelve likes so far. I feel relieved and also kind of gross, like I did it for them, not for me.
Maybe I'll ask Sachin tomorrow if he actually wanted to.
Usha

qa.q: How many times did Usha film the video?
qa.a: Eleven times, in the bathroom.

qa.q: How does Usha feel after posting the video?
qa.a: Usha feels relieved and also kind of gross, sensing it was done to fit in rather than out of wanting to.

qa.q: What might help Usha the next time a trend sweeps the class?
qa.a: Asking whether it is wanted or only done to avoid standing out, and talking honestly with a friend like Sachin who may feel the same.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Sachin to post the trend?
qa.a: Sachin hates dancing too, so he may also have felt pushed into it by everyone else posting.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows joining a class trend they dislike because being the only one left feels unbearable.

passage: In Bhadrachalam, the Class 10 results came out on a Monday, and by Tuesday every girl in Minakshi's group had chosen the science stream. "Obviously MPC," said Ayesha, filling her form at the xerox shop. "Everyone is taking it." Minakshi loved history. She read the old temple inscriptions on her way to tuition and could talk about the Kakatiyas for an hour. But when the shopkeeper asked, "Which stream?", her throat went tight. If she chose arts, she'd be the only one. People would ask why. Her aunts would ask why. She pictured sitting alone in a different classroom. "MPC," she heard herself say. Walking home, the form in her bag felt heavy. That night she opened her history textbook, not the physics one, and read until her mother turned off the light.

qa.q: Which stream did every girl in Minakshi's group choose?
qa.a: Every girl in Minakshi's group had chosen the science stream.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling when the shopkeeper asked which stream?
qa.a: She felt anxious, her throat going tight, afraid of being the only one to choose arts and having to explain why.

qa.q: What could Minakshi do before submitting the form?
qa.a: She could talk to a teacher or her parents about her love of history and ask whether the form can still be changed, instead of just following the group.

qa.q: How does Ayesha seem to see the choice of stream?
qa.a: Ayesha treats science as the obvious choice simply because everyone is taking it.

grounding: Shows a teenager choosing the same study stream as her friends, despite loving history, because standing out makes her anxious.

passage: That winter in Vancouver, every girl in Mei's year wore the same enormous silver puffer jacket. It crinkled when they walked. Mei thought it looked like a baked potato. She had her grandmother's old green wool coat, which she loved. But by November she was the only one in green. In the hallway she felt eyes on her, or thought she did. At lunch someone said, "Retro," and she couldn't tell if it was kind. On Saturday she spent her birthday money on a silver puffer. On Monday she blended in perfectly and felt strangely empty. Felix, from her maths class, was still wearing his orange raincoat, as he did every year. "Where's the green coat?" he asked. "I liked it." Mei looked at the rows of silver and didn't know what to say.

qa.q: What did Mei spend her birthday money on?
qa.a: A silver puffer.

qa.q: What was Mei feeling on Monday wearing the silver puffer?
qa.a: She blended in, but felt strangely empty, because she had given up a coat she loved to avoid standing out.

qa.q: What could Mei ask herself next time a trend takes over?
qa.a: She could ask whether she actually likes the thing, or only fears being the odd one out.

qa.q: How does Felix see Mei's change of coat?
qa.a: Felix misses the green coat and seems puzzled, since he liked it and keeps wearing his own orange raincoat.

grounding: Shows a teenager giving up a coat she loves for a trend jacket because being the only one different makes her anxious.

passage: On Saturday morning at the residential school in Dehradun, word went round the Class 11 hostel: everyone was bunking PT and hiding in the library. "The whole class is in," a girl whispered at breakfast. Vidya's stomach flipped. She actually liked PT. But if forty girls bunked and she turned up alone, the PT sir would ask where everyone was, and they'd all know she had told. Anjali, her roommate, shrugged. "I'm going to PT. I don't care." Vidya followed the crowd into the library, heart thudding, pretending to read. At 9:15 the warden walked in with a register. All forty names went on a list for a letter home. Anjali was the only one who'd played basketball. That night Vidya lay awake, not sure what she'd been more afraid of: the letter, or being the one who stood apart.

qa.q: How many girls went on the warden's list?
qa.a: All forty names went on a list for a letter home.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling as she followed the crowd into the library?
qa.a: She felt anxious, heart thudding, afraid of standing out and being blamed if she went to PT alone.

qa.q: What would you advise Vidya the next time a whole group decides something?
qa.a: Pause and ask what she actually wants, as Anjali did, since the crowd being large doesn't make the choice right or safe.

qa.q: Why might Anjali react differently to the mass bunk?
qa.a: Anjali seems less worried about standing out, so she simply did what she wanted and went to PT.

grounding: Shows a teenager joining a mass bunk because everyone does, anxious about standing out, though she wanted to attend.

passage:
Dear Nazia didi,

You asked why I picked commerce when I've always loved biology. I've been avoiding the answer, but here it is.

When the stream forms came, all five of my friends ticked commerce. Every single one. In the group chat they kept saying, "Commerce gang!" and making plans to sit together in Class 11.

I sat with the form for an hour. My hand kept going to biology. But then I pictured walking into a class where I knew nobody, and my stomach went tight. I didn't want to be the odd one out.

So I ticked commerce.

It's been three weeks. I sit with my friends, which is nice. But in accounts class, I doodle cells in the margins.

I think I chose my friends, not the subject. Can we talk on the phone this weekend? I don't know if it's too late to change.

Trisha

qa.q: How many of Trisha's friends ticked commerce?
qa.a: All five of my friends ticked commerce.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling while sitting with the form?
qa.a: Trisha felt anxious, with a tight stomach, at the thought of walking into a class alone and standing out.

qa.q: What could Trisha do now, and who could help?
qa.a: Trisha could talk with Nazia didi and the school counsellor about whether switching to biology is still possible, and what it would take.

qa.q: How might Trisha's friends react if Trisha switched?
qa.a: The friends might be surprised or a bit sad at first, but real friends would likely stay close outside class.

grounding: A teenager follows friends into a stream that isn't loved because standing out feels frightening.

passage:
You asked about the hair thing last year, Ujjwal? Okay. I'm Wasim. Let me tell you.

In Class 9, almost every boy in our section got the same haircut. Shaved at the sides, long on top. It started with two boys, then ten, then everyone.

I didn't like it. My face looked weird with it. But every day at lunch someone asked, "When are you getting it?" And when I said maybe never, they laughed.

I lay awake worrying about being the only one. It sounds silly now. But it felt huge.

So I got it. Abbu stared at me. My sister laughed so hard she cried.

The worst part was I still didn't like it. I kept touching the sides.

By the next term, half the boys had grown it out. Nobody even remembered.

I don't regret the haircut much. I regret that I couldn't just say, "Not for me."

qa.q: What haircut did almost every boy get?
qa.a: Shaved at the sides, long on top.

qa.q: Why did Wasim get the haircut even without liking it?
qa.a: Wasim felt anxious about being the only one without it and lay awake worrying, so fitting in felt more important than liking it.

qa.q: What could Wasim do the next time a trend comes along?
qa.a: Wasim could pause and ask whether the trend is liked or just feared missing, and practise saying "Not for me" calmly.

qa.q: How might Wasim's sister have seen the haircut?
qa.a: Wasim's sister found it very funny, laughing so hard she cried.

grounding: A teenager gets the haircut the whole class has, though it isn't liked, because standing out feels too risky.

passage:
Monday. The class group chat buzzed: "Mass bunk tomorrow after lunch! Everyone's in!" Ankita wasn't sure. She had a history test on Wednesday and liked that teacher. But forty-two people had replied "in". She typed "in" too, her stomach fluttering.

Tuesday. After lunch, the whole class walked out to the chai shop. Ankita went along, laughing with everyone, but she kept checking the time. Tenzin, her bench-mate, stayed behind. "I just don't want to," he'd said simply.

Friday. The principal called the whole class in. Everyone got a warning note for their parents. The history teacher looked disappointed. Tenzin, alone, got nothing.

On the way home, Ankita asked him, "Weren't you scared? Being the only one?"

"A bit," he admitted. "But I asked myself if I actually wanted to go. I didn't."

Ankita folded the warning note. She hadn't wanted to either. She had just wanted not to be the only one.

qa.q: How many people had replied "in" on Monday?
qa.a: Forty-two people had replied "in".

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when she typed "in"?
qa.a: Ankita felt anxious and unsure, her stomach fluttering, but afraid of being the only one who didn't join.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do that Ankita could learn from?
qa.a: Tenzin asked himself whether he actually wanted to go and acted on the honest answer, even though he stood out.

qa.q: How might the history teacher have felt about the mass bunk?
qa.a: The history teacher felt disappointed, perhaps especially by students like Ankita who usually engaged in class.

grounding: Over a week, a teenager joins a class mass bunk because everyone does, though she didn't want to, and feels anxious about standing out.

passage: Siddharth, you asked why I never studied what I loved. Sit, the diyas on your balcony can wait a minute. When I was fifteen, in Aligarh, every girl in my class signed up for the science stream, because Rukhsana did, and then her whole group did. I loved drawing buildings. I wanted arts, with geography. But standing alone at that form table, with thirty girls watching, my hands went cold. What if they laughed? What if I was the odd one out? So I ticked science. Two years of biology I hated. Rukhsana, it turned out, had only picked science because her cousin had. Much later, at twenty-four, I studied town planning anyway. So when your friends all pick the same thing, you remember Zeenat aunty's two lost years, hmm?

qa.q: Which stream did Zeenat really want at fifteen?
qa.a: Arts, with geography, because she loved drawing buildings.

qa.q: What was young Zeenat feeling at the form table?
qa.a: She felt anxious and exposed, afraid the thirty girls would laugh if she stood out, so ticking science felt safer.

qa.q: What choice at the form table could have changed the story?
qa.a: She could have ticked arts with geography, perhaps after talking to a teacher or family member beforehand, so the choice rested on what she loved rather than on the crowd.

qa.q: Why did Rukhsana pick science, according to the story?
qa.a: Rukhsana had only picked science because her cousin had, so even the person everyone followed was following someone else.

grounding: Shows a teenager choosing a study stream because many peers did, and feeling anxious about standing out.
